title: Roman love - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Drawing on Kyle Harper's From Shame to Sin, the essay argues the myth of tolerant pagan Rome crushed by repressive Christianity is badly incomplete: Roman permissiveness was a selective licence for free men over slaves, and Christianity invented mutual fidelity and extended moral concern to the rightless, while remaining hostile to desire.

insights.claim: Roman sexual permissiveness applied almost only to free men, who could freely have sex with male and female slaves and prostitutes, including children, with no norm of male fidelity.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The 'tolerant antiquity' narrative is a poor baseline for judging how norms change; permissiveness was a status privilege, not a general freedom.
insights.locator: It is true that Roman sexual norms were permissive in some ways

insights.claim: Coerced sex was ubiquitous in the Roman Empire because slave prostitution was widespread even though only a small minority of Romans owned slaves; the price of sex was about that of a loaf of bread.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Illustrates how cheap, unfree labour shapes the economics of sexual markets.
insights.locator: Although only a small minority of Romans owned slaves

insights.claim: Roman tolerance of homosexuality was strictly a licence for free men to penetrate unfree ones; being penetrated was shameful and the Lex Scantinia likely punished men who penetrated free males and men who consented to being penetrated.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Roman norms were organised around status, not orientation, so modern tolerant/repressive framings map poorly onto them.
insights.locator: The norms governing sex between men are more surprising

insights.claim: Female sexuality in Rome was governed by the usual premodern code of virginity at marriage and fidelity afterwards, with tight modesty norms, face veils in Greek-speaking provinces, and contempt for lesbianism.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Shows the double standard that Christianity later partly disrupted.
insights.locator: Roman permissiveness was highly selective, however

insights.claim: Early Christians created the ideal of male fidelity by combining the Jewish prohibition of extramarital sex with Roman monogamy, producing the idea that each man should be faithful to one woman as each woman to one man.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A foundational social norm of Western family structure was a historical invention that could erode with Christianity's decline.
insights.locator: One result was the invention of male fidelity

insights.claim: The author doubts that exclusive mutual fidelity was independently invented in any other major civilization, and wonders whether its hold on Europeans survives Christianity's decline.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Watch for long-run shifts in marriage and fidelity norms as religious affiliation declines.
insights.quote: Perhaps we shall live to know if its hold over the European peoples survives Christianity’s decline.
insights.locator: The novelty of this innovation is hard to overstate

insights.claim: John Chrysostom explicitly attacked the view that adultery means only violating a married woman, condemning a married man's affairs with prostitutes or slave girls, and Pelagius said laws were made by men against women.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Early Christian leaders knowingly broke with prevailing sexual double standards.
insights.quote: The laws were made by men, and they are disposed against women
insights.locator: The early Christians had some sense of their radicalism here

insights.claim: In 428 the Christianized Roman government banned pimps, fathers and slave-owners from selling women for involuntary sex and extended protection to free women forced into prostitution by poverty, directing them to bishops, judges or municipal officials.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: An early example of law restricting coercive exploitation motivated by religious moral concern.
insights.locator: One example was a sustained campaign by the Christianized Empire

insights.claim: Most early Christians accepted slavery unquestioningly despite grounding moral status in relationship to God; Gregory of Nyssa was the great exception and the first recorded abolitionist.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Moral progress from new principles was uneven and slow to be applied.
insights.locator: In theory, Christianity grounds moral status

insights.claim: Christian sexual restrictiveness stemmed partly from negativity about desire and partly from extending moral concern to the rightless people of the classical world, though in practice predatory sexual life often continued under a veneer of Christianization.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Norm change can be real in its effects even when enforcement is weak.
insights.quote: An illusion can become a half-truth, a mask can alter the expression of a face.
insights.locator: In other ways, though, the early Christians seem more complex

insights.claim: Early Christian writers were relentlessly negative about sexual desire, viewing it at best as a morally neutral animal appetite and more commonly as intrinsically sinful, with virginity preferred to marriage and marriage accepted mainly for procreation.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: On desire, the popular image of austere early Christians is accurate.

insights.claim: Only in the Middle Ages did some Christians see parallels between human desire and love of God, such as longing and self-abandonment, and so come to view desire as potentially ennobling.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The romantic view of desire is a later cultural development rooted in religious ideas.
insights.locator: During the Middle Ages, some Christians started to notice
